paragraphs: And so, on that frosty, snowy, windy day in November, Kolya Krassotkin was sitting at home. It was Sunday and there was no school. It had just struck eleven, and he badly wanted to go out “on very urgent business.” But he had been left alone in charge of the house, because all the grown-ups happened to be away, owing to a sudden and unusual event. Madame Krassotkin had rented two small rooms, cut off from the rest of the house by a passage, to a doctor’s wife and her two small children. This lady was the same age as Anna Fyodorovna and a great friend of hers. Her husband, the doctor, had left twelve months earlier, going first to Orenburg and then to Tashkend, and for the last six months she had not heard a word from him. If not for her friendship with Madame Krassotkin, which was some comfort to the abandoned wife, she would surely have dissolved completely in tears. And now, to add to her troubles, Katerina, her only servant, had suddenly announced the evening before, to her mistress’s amazement, that she meant to bring a child into the world before morning. It seemed almost miraculous to everyone that nobody had noticed this was likely. The astounded doctor’s wife decided to move Katerina, while there was still time, to an establishment in town kept by a midwife for such emergencies. Since she valued her servant highly, she carried out this plan at once and stayed there to look after her. By morning, all of Madame Krassotkin’s friendly sympathy and energy were called on, to give assistance and to appeal to someone for help in the matter.

So both ladies were away from home, the Krassotkins’ servant, Agafya, had gone to the market, and Kolya was left for a while to guard and look after “the kids,” that is, the doctor’s wife’s son and daughter, who had been left alone. Kolya wasn’t afraid of minding the house. Besides, he had Perezvon, who had been told to lie flat under the bench in the hall and not move. Every time Kolya, pacing through the rooms, came into the hall, the dog shook his head and gave two loud, hinting taps on the floor with his tail. But alas! the whistle that would release him never sounded. Kolya looked sternly at the luckless dog, who sank back into obedient stiffness. The one thing that worried Kolya was “the kids.” He looked, of course, with the utmost scorn on Katerina’s unexpected adventure, but he was very fond of the bereaved “kiddies,” and had already taken them a picture-book. Nastya, the elder, a girl of eight, could read, and Kostya, the boy, aged seven, loved being read to by her. Krassotkin could, of course, have found more entertaining things for them to do. He could have lined them up side by side and played soldiers, or sent them off to hide all over the house. He had done so more than once before and wasn’t above doing it. In fact, a report once spread at school that Krassotkin played horses with the little lodgers at home, prancing with his head to one side like a trace-horse. But Krassotkin haughtily parried this jab. He pointed out that to play horses with boys of one’s own age, boys of thirteen, would certainly be disgraceful “at this date,” but that he did it for “the kids,” because he liked them, and no one had a right to call him to account for his feelings. The two “kids” adored him.

But this time he was in no mood for games. He had some very important business of his own ahead of him, something almost mysterious. Meanwhile time was passing, and Agafya, who could have taken over the children, still hadn’t come back from the market. He had already crossed the passage several times, opened the door of the lodgers’ room and looked anxiously in at “the kids,” who were sitting over the book, as he had told them to. Every time he opened the door they grinned at him, hoping he would come in and do something delightful and amusing. But Kolya was bothered, and he didn’t go in.

At last it struck eleven, and he made up his mind once and for all that if that “damned” Agafya wasn’t back within ten minutes, he would go out without waiting for her. He would make “the kids” promise, of course, to be brave while he was away, not to be naughty, and not to cry from fright. With this plan, he put on his wadded winter overcoat with its catskin fur collar and slung his satchel over his shoulder. His mother was forever begging him to put on galoshes in such cold weather, but he ignored her pleas: he gave the galoshes a contemptuous look as he crossed the hall and went out in his boots alone. Perezvon, seeing him in his outdoor clothes, began tapping nervously but vigorously on the floor with his tail. Twitching all over, he even let out a plaintive whine. But Kolya, seeing his dog’s passionate excitement, decided it was a breach of discipline. He kept him under the bench for another minute, and only when he had opened the door into the passage did he whistle for him. The dog leapt up like a mad creature and rushed ahead of him, bounding with delight.

Kolya opened the door to peep in at “the kids.” They were both sitting at the table as before, not reading but arguing hotly about something. The children often argued together about the various exciting problems of life, and Nastya, being the elder, always got the best of it. If Kostya didn’t agree with her, he almost always appealed to Kolya Krassotkin, and both of them regarded his verdict as final. This time the “kids’” discussion interested Krassotkin quite a bit, and he stood still in the passage to listen. The children saw that he was listening, and that made them argue with even greater energy.

“I’ll never, never believe,” Nastya prattled, “that old women find babies among the cabbages in the kitchen-garden. It’s winter now and there are no cabbages, so the old woman couldn’t have brought Katerina a daughter.”
Kolya whistled to himself.
“Or maybe they do bring babies from somewhere, but only to people who are married.”
Kostya stared at Nastya and listened, thinking it over very deeply.
“Nastya, how silly you are!” he said at last, firmly and calmly. “How can Katerina have a baby when she isn’t married?”
Nastya was exasperated.
“You don’t know anything about it,” she snapped irritably. “Maybe she has a husband, only he’s in prison, so now she’s got a baby.”
“But is her husband in prison?” the matter-of-fact Kostya asked gravely.

“Or, I’ll tell you what,” Nastya broke in impulsively, completely rejecting and forgetting her first idea. “She hasn’t got a husband, you’re right about that, but she wants to be married, so she’s been thinking about getting married, and thinking and thinking about it, till now she’s got it, that is, not a husband but a baby.”
“Well, maybe so,” Kostya agreed, totally beaten. “But you didn’t say so before. So how could I know?”
“Come on, kiddies,” said Kolya, stepping into the room. “You’re terrible people, I see.”
“And Perezvon with you!” grinned Kostya, and he began snapping his fingers and calling Perezvon.
“I’m in a difficulty, kids,” Krassotkin began solemnly, “and you must help me. Agafya must have broken her leg, since she hasn’t turned up yet, that’s certain. I have to go out. Will you let me go?”
The children looked anxiously at each other. Their smiling faces showed signs of uneasiness, but they didn’t yet fully grasp what was expected of them.
“You won’t be naughty while I’m gone? You won’t climb on the cupboard and break your legs? You won’t be scared alone and cry?”
A look of deep gloom came over the children’s faces.
“And I could show you something as a reward, a little copper cannon that can be fired with real gunpowder.”
The children’s faces brightened at once. “Show us the cannon,” said Kostya, beaming all over.
Krassotkin put his hand in his satchel, pulled out a little bronze cannon and stood it on the table.
“Ah, you’re bound to ask that! Look, it’s on wheels.” He rolled the toy along the table. “And it can be fired, too. It can be loaded with shot and fired.”
“And it could kill someone?”

“It can kill anyone; you’ve only got to aim at somebody,” and Krassotkin explained where the powder had to go and where the shot should be rolled in. He showed them a tiny hole like a touch-hole, and told them that it kicked when it was fired.
The children listened with intense interest. What struck their imagination most was that the cannon kicked.
“And do you have any powder?” Nastya asked.
“Yes.”
“Show us the powder, too,” she drawled with a pleading smile.

Krassotkin dived into his satchel again and pulled out a small flask holding a little real gunpowder. He had some shot, too, in a twist of paper. He even uncorked the flask and shook a little powder into the palm of his hand.
“You have to be careful there’s no fire around, or it would blow up and kill us all,” Krassotkin warned them dramatically.
The children gazed at the powder with an awestruck alarm that only made their enjoyment keener. But Kostya liked the shot better.
“And does the shot burn?” he asked.
“No, it doesn’t.”
“Give me a little shot,” he begged in a pleading voice.
“I’ll give you a little shot; here, take it, but don’t show it to your mother till I’m back, or she’ll be sure to think it’s gunpowder, and she’ll die of fright and give you a thrashing.”
“Mother never does whip us,” Nastya remarked at once.
“I know, I only said it to finish the sentence. And don’t you ever deceive your mother, except just this once, until I get back. So, kiddies, can I go out? You won’t be scared and cry when I’m gone?”
“We sha—all cry,” drawled Kostya, already on the verge of tears.
“We’ll cry, we’ll be sure to cry,” Nastya chimed in with timid haste.
“Oh, children, children, how full of danger your years are! There’s no help for it, chickens, I’ll have to stay with you, I don’t know how long. And time is passing, time is passing, oogh!”
“Tell Perezvon to play dead!” Kostya begged.
“There’s no help for it, we have to turn to Perezvon. _Ici_, Perezvon.” And Kolya began giving orders to the dog, who performed all his tricks.

He was a rough-haired dog of medium size, with a coat of a sort of lilac-gray color. He was blind in his right eye, and his left ear was torn. He whined and jumped, stood and walked on his hind legs, and lay on his back with his paws in the air, stiff as though he were dead. While this last trick was going on, the door opened and Agafya, Madame Krassotkin’s servant, a stout woman of forty, pitted with smallpox, appeared in the doorway. She had come back from the market with a bag full of provisions in her hand. Holding up the bag in her left hand, she stood still to watch the dog. Kolya had been so anxious for her to return, yet he didn’t cut the performance short. After keeping Perezvon dead for the usual time, he finally whistled to him. The dog jumped up and began bounding about for joy at having done his duty.
“Imagine, a dog!” Agafya remarked sententiously.
“Why are you late, female?” asked Krassotkin sternly.
“Female, indeed! Go on with you, you brat.”
“Brat?”

“Yes, a brat. What’s it to you if I’m late? If I’m late, you can be sure I have good reason,” muttered Agafya, busying herself at the stove, without a trace of anger or displeasure in her voice. She seemed quite pleased, in fact, to have a skirmish with her merry young master.

“Listen, you frivolous young woman,” Krassotkin began, getting up from the sofa, “can you swear by everything you hold sacred in the world, and something else besides, that you’ll watch the kids carefully while I’m gone? I’m going out.”
“And what am I going to swear for?” laughed Agafya. “I’ll look after them without that.”
“No, you must swear on your eternal salvation. Otherwise I won’t go.”
“Well, don’t, then. What does it matter to me? It’s cold out; stay at home.”

“Kids,” Kolya turned to the children, “this woman will stay with you till I come back or till your mother comes, since she should have been back long ago. She’ll give you some lunch, too. You’ll give them something, Agafya, won’t you?”
“That I can do.”

“Good-by, chickens, I go with my heart at rest. And you, granny,” he added gravely, in an undertone, as he passed Agafya, “I hope you’ll spare their tender years and not tell them any of your old woman’s nonsense about Katerina. _Ici_, Perezvon!”
“Get along with you!” retorted Agafya, really angry this time. “Ridiculous boy! You want a whipping for saying such things, that’s what you want!”
